heading: Safety rules that stop the build
body: Tachyon refuses four common and dangerous mistakes when it builds, the way it refuses a file with two classes (ADR 0068). No setting turns them off. First, every route says who may call it (see Who may call a route). Second, no password, token or key is written in the code, a template or public settings: Tachyon recognizes the usual shapes of AWS, Google, Azure, GitHub, Stripe and Slack keys, private keys, JSON Web Tokens, and a long random text given to a name such as `password`, `secret`, `token` or `apiKey`. Put the value in `.env` with a `YON_` name and read it through the Yon settings; code that runs in the browser gets no secrets at all. Third, code never runs a text as code (`eval`, `new Function`, Python `exec`, Ruby `instance_eval` with a text, PHP `eval`, a Java `ScriptEngine`, C# scripting), and it never joins values into query text: write the query as one text or an UPPER_CASE constant and pass the values in the parameter list. Redis keys and values are always parameters. Fourth, code sends requests only to the hosts that you list, `tac.outgoing.hosts` for page code and `outgoing.hosts` in `server/application.json` for Yon code. This stops server-side request forgery (SSRF): a caller cannot make your app call an address that they choose. At run time the browser refuses other hosts, because Tachyon adds the listed hosts to the page's `connect-src` security rule, and Yon code sends its requests through a local guard that refuses other hosts. The guard works for every HTTP client that reads the standard proxy settings (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`): JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Ruby, PHP with cURL, Go, C# and Rust with reqwest. The Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Dart clients read them only when you ask them to (`ProxySelector.getDefault()`, `HttpClient.findProxyFromEnvironment`); for a hard limit on every language, run Yon with Firecracker isolation and its egress setting.
